title_original: Ranti Bam’s Black Ifa in Venice Biennale’s In Minor Keys.

blocks.text: At the Arsenale in Venice, Ranti Bam’s five sculptures, Ifa Ile Oja – Black Ifa , explore the relationship between body, memory and spirituality as part of the 61st Venice Biennale, In Minor Keys .

For Ranti Bam, clay is more than a material. It is a vessel for memory, an extension of the body and a means of engaging with the unseen. Through forms that challenge conventional ideas of containment, her practice explores vulnerability, transformation and the possibilities of holding and being held.

In this conversation with ART AFRICA , Bam reflects on the intuitive processes behind her sculptures, the spiritual resonances of Ifá and the importance of allowing art to remain open to interpretation. Presented at the Arsenale as part of In Minor Keys , her work offers a meditation on materiality, freedom and the quiet power of paying attention. Installation view of Ranti Bam,’ Ifa Ile Oja – Black Ifa ‘ at the Arsenale at the 61st Biennale di Venezia , 2026. Image courtesy of the artist and James Cohan, New York. Photograph by Casey Kelbaugh / CKA.

blocks.caption: Installation view of Ranti Bam,’ Ifa Ile Oja – Black Ifa ‘ at the Arsenale at the 61st Biennale di Venezia , 2026. Image courtesy of the artist and James Cohan, New York. Photograph by Casey Kelbaugh / CKA.

blocks.text: Suzette Bell-Roberts: Your artistic practice explores the relationship between clay, the body, memory, and spirituality. How has your understanding of these connections evolved, and how do they shape the forms you create?

Ranti Bam: I’ve come to see these things as increasingly inseparable. The body holds memory, clay holds memory, and both are constantly being shaped by touch, pressure, time and experience. My work keeps returning to questions of freedom and containment. What does it mean to hold something? How do we hold ourselves, our histories, one another? Clay allows me to explore these questions physically, while making room for things we can sense but cannot always articulate. Installation view of Ranti Bam,’ Ifa Ile Oja – Black Ifa ‘ at the Arsenale at the 61st Biennale di Venezia , 2026. Image courtesy of the artist and James Cohan, New York. Photograph by Casey Kelbaugh / CKA.

blocks.caption: Installation view of Ranti Bam,’ Ifa Ile Oja – Black Ifa ‘ at the Arsenale at the 61st Biennale di Venezia , 2026. Image courtesy of the artist and James Cohan, New York. Photograph by Casey Kelbaugh / CKA.

blocks.text: Your sculptures challenge traditional ideas of what a vessel should look like or how it should function. What draws you to the vessel as an artistic form, and how do you explore its relationship to the human body?

For me, a vessel is anything with the capacity to hold. It doesn’t need to be hollow or enclosed. A flat surface can hold an impression, a word can hold meaning, a person can hold memory. I began working with vessels in the round because they communicate so completely the relationship between interior and exterior, openness and boundary, conditions we also experience within our bodies. I’m less interested in function than in the possibility that containment itself can be liberating. The vessel’s fragility is also deeply human. It can protect, but it can break. I believe all flaws are beautiful, not despite their imperfections, but because of them. Ranti Bam, ‘ Ifa 1 ‘, 2026, Handbuilt black stoneware, © Ranti Bam 2026. Courtesy of the artist and Norr Cohan, New York. Photo by Jacob Friis-Holm Nielsen.

blocks.caption: Ranti Bam, ‘ Ifa 1 ‘, 2026, Handbuilt black stoneware, © Ranti Bam 2026. Courtesy of the artist and Norr Cohan, New York. Photo by Jacob Friis-Holm Nielsen.

blocks.text: Your work draws on Yoruba spiritual traditions, particularly the concept of Ifa , which relates to divination and connection. How has your engagement with these traditions shaped your artistic language and understanding of clay?
I don’t necessarily begin with Yoruba spirituality as a point of departure. These connections often reveal themselves through making.

The first Ifa emerged from an attempt to create totems. I’d made the clay columns but realised I no longer wanted to make totems, although I wasn’t quite sure what I wanted instead. Three nights later, I returned to the studio and fell into the work. That’s how the series began. What drew me to Ifá was its spiritual practice of communing with the divine, and equally, the meaning of drawing close. Both resonate deeply with my relationship with clay, the intimacy of making, and the possibility of connecting with something beyond ourselves. Ranti Bam, ‘ Ifa 2′, 2026, Handbuilt black stoneware, © Ranti Bam 2026. Courtesy of the artist and Norr Cohan, New York. Photo by Jacob Friis-Holm Nielsen.

blocks.caption: Ranti Bam, ‘ Ifa 2′, 2026, Handbuilt black stoneware, © Ranti Bam 2026. Courtesy of the artist and Norr Cohan, New York. Photo by Jacob Friis-Holm Nielsen.

blocks.text: At the 2026 Venice Biennale, you present five sculptures titled Ifa Ile Oja – Black Ifa , which take on the presence of guardians. What informed these works, and how do you understand their relationship to the space and the people who encounter them?
I understand why the sculptures might be seen as guardians, but I prefer to leave their identities open.

For me, the majesty of art lies in the metaphorical space it creates for our imaginations and longings to wander. I consider this the most vital part of art-making and take great care not to interfere with it. We each bring our own histories and desires to what we encounter, and I find it beautiful that a work can hold all these possibilities without insisting on any one meaning. Ranti Bam, ‘ Ifa 3′, 2026, Handbuilt black stoneware, © Ranti Bam 2026. Courtesy of the artist and Norr Cohan, New York. Photo by Jacob Friis-Holm Nielsen.

blocks.caption: Ranti Bam, ‘ Ifa 3′, 2026, Handbuilt black stoneware, © Ranti Bam 2026. Courtesy of the artist and Norr Cohan, New York. Photo by Jacob Friis-Holm Nielsen.

blocks.text: In your creative process, you maintain a close physical relationship with clay, allowing the material to respond to your movements and gestures. How does this interaction shape the final form of your sculptures, and what role does the unexpected play in your practice?

Over the years, clay and I have developed a deep symbiosis. I don’t work from preparatory drawings. I begin with an intention, an idea, and the forms emerge through making. As my work has grown in scale, my gestures have shifted from hugging and holding to manipulating and supporting…and I’m still trying to flesh out the words. I’m fascinated by this negotiation between my intentions and the material’s own possibilities and limitations. Weight, gravity, pressure and balance all have a part to play. The unexpected is fundamental to my practice. Often, what emerges beyond my intentions is far more interesting than anything I could have imagined. Ranti Bam, ‘ Ifa 4′, 2026, Handbuilt black stoneware, © Ranti Bam 2026. Courtesy of the artist and Norr Cohan, New York. Photo by Jacob Friis-Holm Nielsen.

blocks.caption: Ranti Bam, ‘ Ifa 4′, 2026, Handbuilt black stoneware, © Ranti Bam 2026. Courtesy of the artist and Norr Cohan, New York. Photo by Jacob Friis-Holm Nielsen.

blocks.text: The 2026 Venice Biennale, In Minor Keys , conceived by Koyo Kouoh, invites audiences to consider quieter forms of expression, listening, and connection. How do you interpret this theme in relation to your practice, especially your exploration of spirituality, materiality, and the unseen?

What I find beautiful about In Minor Keys is its invitation to pay attention to what might otherwise go unnoticed. There is a generosity in making space for quieter ways of being, knowing and experiencing the world.

My relationship with clay is rooted in this attentiveness. Making requires listening, patience and a willingness to allow things to emerge in their own time. I think there’s something particularly moving about Koyo’s vision in a world so preoccupied with visibility and certainty, and with conflating visibility with value. Not everything needs to announce or explain itself. Sometimes it’s enough to create the conditions for something to be experienced. Ranti Bam, ‘ Ifa 5′, 2026, Handbuilt black stoneware, © Ranti Bam 2026. Courtesy of the artist and Norr Cohan, New York. Photo by Jacob Friis-Holm Nielsen.

blocks.caption: Ranti Bam, ‘ Ifa 5′, 2026, Handbuilt black stoneware, © Ranti Bam 2026. Courtesy of the artist and Norr Cohan, New York. Photo by Jacob Friis-Holm Nielsen.

blocks.text: Your sculptures at the Arsenale create a dialogue between clay, architecture, and histories of making. How did the Arsenale setting shape your presentation, and what conversations do you hope emerge between the works and their surroundings?

There’s something beautiful about exhibiting clay within a building itself made from earth, transformed by human hands. The Arsenale carries its own histories of labour, production and time. Its scale and material presence made me consider how the sculptures might inhabit the space rather than simply occupy it.

I don’t necessarily want to prescribe the conversation between the works and their surroundings. I prefer to let these different histories coexist, leaving room for people to make their own connections. Installation view of Ranti Bam,’ Ifa Ile Oja – Black Ifa ‘ at the Arsenale at the 61st Biennale di Venezia , 2026. Image courtesy of the artist and James Cohan, New York. blocks.text: Your work explores vulnerability, transformation, and the relationship between the physical and spiritual worlds. What does participating in the 61st Venice Biennale mean to you at this stage of your career, and how do you see your practice contributing to the wider conversations of In Minor Keys ?

I’ve never thought much about having a creative career. I’m far more interested in living a creative life and being present to it. I hope my work offers others something of that freedom, to wander, imagine and find their own possibilities in the seemingly ordinary.
